overview:
Around 1200 BCE the palace kingdoms of Mycenaean Greece came apart. Their citadels burned or were abandoned, the Linear B script used to tally sheep and chariot wheels fell out of use, and long-distance trade in the metals that made bronze thinned out. The same decades saw the Hittite empire and the port city of Ugarit fail, so whatever happened in the Aegean was part of a wider eastern Mediterranean unravelling. The four centuries that followed are conventionally called the Greek Dark Age, a label that says more about the absence of writing than about the absence of life: excavation at Lefkandi on Euboea has turned up a wealthy eleventh-century burial and imports from Cyprus, Egypt and the Levant, and regions such as Attica show modest continuity. Iron, available locally, replaced bronze. Out of this fallow stretch came the alphabet, borrowed from Phoenician traders, and the poems attributed to Homer.

From roughly the eighth century the characteristic Greek form took shape: the polis, a small self-governing city and its farmland, fiercely independent and endlessly at odds with its neighbours. Greeks planted hundreds of settlements from the Black Sea to Sicily, southern Italy and the coast of France, spreading their language, coinage and pottery along the shipping lanes. The Archaic period ended with two Persian invasions, in 490 and 480 BCE, repelled by improbable coalitions of city-states; the Classical period that followed compressed into about a century and a half the Athenian democracy, tragedy and comedy, the Parthenon, Herodotus and Thucydides, Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, and the long, exhausting Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta. Macedon, on the northern fringe and long regarded as half-barbarian by southern Greeks, absorbed them all under Philip II, and his son Alexander carried Greek arms as far as the Indus between 334 and 323 BCE.

Alexander's death broke his conquests into the successor kingdoms of his generals — Ptolemaic Egypt, the Seleucids in the Near East, the Antigonids in Macedonia — and made Greek the working language of an enormous zone stretching to Afghanistan. Alexandria's library and museum, Euclid, Archimedes and Eratosthenes belong to this Hellenistic age, as does a sculpture far more emotional and theatrical than Classical restraint allowed. Rome moved east steadily, sacking Corinth in 146 BCE and annexing Ptolemaic Egypt in 30 BCE, but the conquest was cultural traffic in both directions: Roman elites learned Greek, copied Greek statues and studied in Athens. Greek remained the language of the eastern Mediterranean, of the New Testament, and eventually of the Byzantine state. The span is usually closed around the sixth century CE, marked symbolically by Justinian's suppression of the philosophical school at Athens in 529.
significance: Much of what later Europe and the Islamic world argued about, they argued about in vocabulary the Greeks invented — democracy, tyranny, politics, physics, history, tragedy, philosophy itself. Greek geometry and astronomy passed through Syriac and Arabic translation into medieval science and were still the working framework when Copernicus and Galileo set out to revise them; Aristotle organised university teaching for centuries. Athenian citizen government, narrow and slave-holding as it was, became the reference point that later revolutionaries and constitution-writers reached for. And the Hellenistic diffusion of Greek across Egypt, Syria and Central Asia set the linguistic conditions for Roman administration in the east, for the spread of early Christianity, and for a thousand years of Byzantine continuity — an inheritance later claimed, selectively and often self-servingly, as the origin of "the West."
coverage: Written from reference syntheses rather than specialist scholarship, and the dataset holds no events at all for this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped place or date. The underlying record is very unevenly distributed: roughly 1200–800 BCE has no contemporary texts and rests entirely on archaeology, one recent study argues most of the destructions conventionally dated to the 1200 BCE collapse are misdated or assumed, and even the Classical period survives mainly through Athenian male authors, leaving Sparta, women, enslaved people, the non-Greek majority of the Hellenistic kingdoms and most of the Roman-era provinces thinly and often hostilely documented.
